title: Amber Alert for the Red Panda - Nepali Times
description: Amber Alert for the Red Panda  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Which panda came first: the Giant Panda in China or the Red Panda in Nepal?

Although the Giant Panda is better known worldwide, the Red Panda was first described by Western scientists in 1825 and given the scientific name Ailurus fulgens . It took another 50 years for the Giant Panda to be scientifically classified even though it is now the celebrity mammal in zoos across the world.

After DNA analysis concluded that the giant panda was actually from the Ursidae bear family, scientists found out that the red panda belonged to a unique taxonomical family called Ailuridae , closer to raccoons and squirrels.

The name ‘panda’ is actually derived from words in a dialect in eastern Nepal ‘nigalya panja’ which means ‘bamboo paw’. Although scientists have studied this shy and elusive mammal for 200 years, very little is still known about its habits and habitat on the forest canopy.

There are said to be only about 1,000 red pandas in Nepal, most of them in the lush cloud forests of eastern Nepal where the thin bamboo called nigalo grows in an altitude belt between 2,400m-3,900m. Although the panda is a carnivore, its favourite snack is bamboo shoots.

Nepali scientists are making progress studying the behaviour of the red panda from a research centre in Taplejung. The findings are important because the mammal is an indicator species that points to the health of the forest ecosystem where it lives.

“Nepal has been successful in receiving global funding but there is a need for a more systematic research method,” says Anusha Pahari of WWF India. She participated at the Red Panda Symposium 2026 organised by Red Panda Network in collaboration with Rotterdam Zoo, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), and the AZA SAFE Red Panda Program earlier this month in Kathmandu.

Protecting the red panda means safeguarding the forest ecosystem on which the animal depends, and working with the communities where the animals roam.

Besides habitat fragmentation and disturbance from new infrastructure, red pandas are also poached and traded for their fur. Disease adds another threat.

Conservationists at the Kathmandu symposium emphasised that protecting the animal means addressing these pressures together, rather than treating forest loss, wildlife trade, and disease as separate problems.

“Fragmented habitats is a major threat for red pandas, and there is an urgent need to identify potential corridors and increase connectivity and water sources so that their population is not affected,” explains Damber Bista of Red Panda Network.

Funding for nature conservation work worldwide is shrinking, and this has also affected resources for research into red pandas. Experts say the challenge is not simply to launch conservation activities, but to keep them going and connect research with work on the ground.

Many rural households across the red panda range from Taplejung to Dolpo in Nepal depend on community forests for their livelihood. Conservation must therefore extend beyond protected areas into landscapes shared by people and wildlife.

“Habitat fragmentation could affect the genetic diversity of

red pandas, and this means we have to be extra careful that human-induced activities do not affect them,” says Pahari.

Another threat for red pandas is from feral dogs which can transmit rabies, and conservation activity has included vaccinating over 10,000 free-ranging community dogs in rural Nepal.

CHARISMATIC SPECIES

Estimates for the red panda population in Nepal have varied widely, researchers have analysed faecal samples to estimate the population which has increased over the years to about 1,000 after the animals were also found in Bhojpur, and as far west as Dolpo. Scientists have also catalogued 72 bamboo species which the pandas eat.

Research gaps remain, however, especially in western Nepal. There is also limited awareness of the animal’s conservation needs. The range of population estimates highlights why a clearer picture matters. Surveys help establish where red pandas live, and spread awareness beyond them just being a charismatic species.

“There is growing awareness for wildlife conservation, but most of it goes to saving larger species like tigers and wild elephants, overshadowing small mammals such as the red panda,” says Pahari.

For communities living alongside red pandas, conservation starts in the forests that sustain their livelihoods and shelter wildlife. Ecotourism and habitat restoration offer ways to connect protection with local livelihoods, giving communities a stake in the animal’s future.

“Close engagement with the community is vital for awareness and conservation, not just for red pandas but nature conservation overall. Local stewardship is the only way in Nepal where people live in close proximity to wildlife,” says Nishan KC from WWF Nepal, which also works in cross-border collaboration since the red panda habitat spans Nepal to India and China.

The red panda’s future is tied to the forests and to the people who depend on them. Giving communities the knowledge and resources to protect that shared home is essential to helping people and red pandas coexist.

Says KC: “Whether it is patrolling for poaching control or any other awareness effort, conservation is something that should happen continuously, it cannot stop.”

publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Prime Minister (PM) Balendra Shah has said the government will introduce necessary policy and regulatory reforms to promote Nepal’s game development and information technology (IT) sectors, creating an environment for domestic companies to expand internationally and emerge as global unicorns.

In a social media post on Friday, Prime Minister Shah said the government would review existing regulations and requirements to facilitate the growth of the sectors.

He highlighted the international success of gaming applications developed by Nepali companies, citing Ludo, which has recorded approximately 200 million downloads worldwide, and Callbreak, with more than 150 million downloads. The Prime Minister also noted growing interest among young Nepalis in game development.

“We reached out to them to understand their challenges and discussed ways to simplify the game development sector and advance it as an industry. We have now begun groundwork to address their concerns,” Shah said.

He added that Nepal’s IT products and service exports were performing well and that the government was working to improve the business environment by reviewing policies related to revenue generation, reinvestment opportunities, taxation and international income.

Shah also said the government would invest in strengthening the broader ecosystem to support IT products and the gaming industry. Initiatives such as game jams, startup events and hackathons will be promoted, alongside regular consultations with stakeholders from the IT sector, Nepal Rastra Bank and the Ministry of Finance, he added.

title: Nepal detains journalists to warn rest of free press - Nepali Times
description: Nepal detains journalists to warn rest of free press  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Whenever Nepal's autocrats wanted to warn the media during the absolute monarchy days, they arrested a few journalists on a Friday.

That is what the state apparatus did on 30 October, leading to muted protests over the weekend. Plainclothes police officers entered newsrooms to nab reporters following a story about state highhandedness.

Photo: ANUP TAMU / FACEBOOK

In the past, authoritarian regimes wanted everyone to know they were behind the detention, but Prime Minister Balendra Shah's office denied any involvement, insinuating that Nepal Police chief Inspector General Dan Bahadur Karki was miffed about media coverage regarding efforts to sack him.

But then on Friday night, the Police said it had been acting on the advisers' orders. For journalists covering their colleagues' detention, this was an impossible to verify case of he-said-she-said.

Even so, it was yet another indication that relations between the governing party and the government are not well. Worse, it could even be a worrying rift between the government and the security apparatus.

All photos: BIKAR RAUNIYAR

Plainclothes police officers made rounds of several media outlets across Kathmandu to question and detain journalists on Friday in a move that was widely condemned by the mediasphere, civil society, political leadership, and press freedom watchdogs.

Security officials took DNA Khabar editor-in-chief Dhiraj Basnet, Motive News editor Shobhraj Baral, and Nepal Press reporter Bishwamani Subedi into custody on Friday afternoon.

Subedi was said to have been detained on the basis of a letter from the Cyber Bureau after Nepal Press published news claiming that the government was considering relieving Inspector General Karki from his duties. Nepal Press newsroom leadership were questioned about their sources.

Basnet was called in by the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office under the pretext of discussing an eSewa account number. Baral was similarly taken in without charges on vague grounds.

Officers also entered the Naya Patrika newsroom in an attempt to find journalist Nawaraj Mainali, who reported on the leaked WhatsApp coversation between a power broker and a Supreme Court justice.

Another police team went to Anamnagar to Diyo Post’s office looking for editor-in-chief Sudeep Bishwakarma and news coordinator Madan Dhungana, but left after failing to find them.

When pressed by journalists on the charge and documentation, police refused to provide them saying they were just acting on ‘orders from above’.

Naya Patrika broke the story earlier this week involving leaked correspondence between Supreme Court Justice Hari Phuyal and political fixer Imam Sapkota insinuating political interference in judicial proceedings. Other media outlets followed up on the piece, with coverage of corruption and collusion between judicial officials, political and security officials, as well as middlemen.

Detained journalists were released after a few hours, reinforcing the theory that this was to send a warning to the rest of the media not to step out of lione.

It is most likely that the PMO ordered the detentions despite denials by the prime minister's advisers. But it was condemned by figures across the political spectrum, most tellingly by leaders of the governing RSP itself. Spokesperson Jagdish Kharel, himself a former tv anchor, said the arrests violated press freedom and freedom of expression.

Many including in the press drew comparisons to the crackdowns on the press during Gyanendra’s rule after he staged a military-backed coup on 1 February 2005 when he sent the army into newsrooms to censor content, and detain pro-democracy journalists.

In a statement, the Federation of Nepalese Journalists called the detention of reporters by polics a blatant interference with press freedom’: ‘It is entirely inappropriate to resort to state terror if there are any grievances about news content instead of seeking resolution through established legal procedures. These actions violate the Constitution, domestic laws, and international legal standards.’

This is not the first time intimidation tactics against the press have been employed since the RSP government took office. In July, there was a coordinated blockade of the main gates of some media companies by illegally parked cars as a symbolic protest against the media coverage of the government's drives to curb traffic violations.

The RSP condemned the move then too, but social media accounts known to be associated with the Prime Minister's chief adviser supported the action. Nepal rans highest in South Asia for press freedom, however trolling and threats against journalists by the prime minister's supporters have led to a degree of self-censorship.

On Friday evening, Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s press adviser Deepa Dahal wrote on social media that the PM, his secretariat, and the PMO had no knowledge of the reporters’ detention, and that the PM had immediately instructed relevant authorities to release the detained journalists and refrain from newsroom crackdowns.

The reporters were released on Friday evening, and the Nepal Police also issued a clarification saying that the journalists were not detained, but brought in for 'routine questioning' on orders from the prime minister's office.

The denial of responsibility by the PMO and the security apparatus points to a disconnect, at least in public, between the two state institutions, at a time when the judicial arm of the state has also been dragged into the mud.

This seems to be an attempt at plausible deniability and finger pointing by the PMO and Police, and hints at a widening rift between Prime Minister Shah and The RSP Chair Rabi Lamichhane.

title: Nepal and Mauritius move closer to G2G labour agreement - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal and Mauritius move closer to G2G labour agreement  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal and Mauritius have moved closer to signing a bilateral labour agreement that would allow Nepali workers to be recruited through a government-to-government (G2G) mechanism.

The High Commission of Mauritius in New Delhi formally conveyed its agreement to Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on October 29, forwarding a revised draft of the proposed memorandum of understanding (MoU) to facilitate the recruitment of Nepali workers through the G2G system.

The proposed agreement aims to expand employment opportunities for Nepali workers in manufacturing, construction, agriculture, tourism and information technology, offering competitive salaries and benefits. It also seeks to promote safe and dignified foreign employment under the Employers Pay Principle, which requires employers, rather than workers, to bear recruitment costs.

The revised draft includes provisions for a government-led recruitment process, the selection of skilled and trained workers, and recruitment procedures in line with the laws of both countries. It also outlines employers’ responsibilities, workers’ rights and welfare provisions, and arrangements for repatriating workers after their employment contracts expire or are terminated.

The initiative follows a bilateral meeting between Nepal’s Minister for Youth, Labour and Employment Ramji Yadav and Mauritius’s Minister of Labour and Industrial Relations Mohamed Reza Cassam Uteem in Geneva, Switzerland, on June 9.

At the meeting, Yadav proposed expanding labour cooperation through a G2G mechanism. Uteem said that employers in Mauritius covered recruitment costs and expressed interest in creating more employment opportunities for Nepali workers.

He also proposed organising an international employment fair in Nepal to facilitate recruitment and strengthen labour cooperation between the two countries.

The Nepali government is now preparing to complete the necessary domestic procedures to finalise the revised draft MoU and move ahead with the proposed agreement.

The initiative is part of Nepal’s broader effort to strengthen labour diplomacy and diversify overseas employment destinations while reducing the costs and risks associated with foreign recruitment.
